title: Longest Increasing Subsequence in O(n log n)
excerpt: The patience-sorting solution to LIS: why the tails array works, why its contents are not the answer, and how binary search replaces the quadratic scan.
seoTitle: Longest Increasing Subsequence in O(n log n) — Explained
seoDescription: A full walkthrough of the O(n log n) longest increasing subsequence algorithm: the tails array, why binary search applies, and the classic off-by-one that breaks it.

content.text: Given an array, find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence, the set of values that appear in order, though not necessarily next to each other. In
It's easy to come up with a quadratic solution using two for loops, but there exists an

The O(n²) dynamic program asks "what is the longest run ending here?" and rescans everything before it. The faster method inverts the question to "for each length, what is the smallest value a run of that length can end on?" That array is sorted by construction, so binary search applies, and its length is the answer even though its contents usually are not.

content.text: In this example, the array tails is a valid solution to the increasing subsequence problem, but that is NOT ALWAYS the case. What is always true, is that the length of the array of tails is the length of the longest increasing subsequence.
Python has the binary search in the standard library; the other two spell it out. All three are the same algorithm.

content.text: Each of the n values is handled once. The work per value is a binary search over
, which never holds more than n entries, so each search is O(log n). Appending and overwriting are both
The quadratic version does O(n) work per element instead of O(log n). At
that is the difference between roughly 1.7 million operations and 10 billion, which is ~5800x more efficient!

items.text: Using upper bound instead of lower bound. That accepts equal values as extensions and silently solves the non-decreasing problem. [7, 7, 7, 7] should answer 1, not 4 — it is the fastest way to catch this.
Returning the contents of tails as the subsequence. The length is always right; the array usually is not a real subsequence.
Appending when the search lands on the last index. Appending is only correct when the index is past the end, meaning no existing entry was large enough.
Forgetting the empty input. An empty array has length 0, and tails is naturally empty, so the base case needs no special handling — but the quadratic version's max() call does.
